title: Why do we get goosebumps?
hook: On a frightened cat, bristling fur puts on a show. On us, with hardly any fur, all that’s left is goosebumps.
summary: Tiny muscles attached to each hair contract and lift it; in furry animals this holds in warmth, and a 2020 study in mice found the same muscles and nerves help hair grow.
cardText: Each hair has a tiny muscle that stands it up when it contracts, raising a little bump. In furry animals this traps warmth; what it does for us is still debated.

cardBlocks.text: Picture a cat cornered by a dog: fur on end, back arched, body turned sideways. All of it makes the cat look bigger. Human goosebumps run on the same machinery, in skin with almost no fur. Every hair has a tiny muscle attached, the arrector pili. In the cold, nerves of the sympathetic system send a signal, the muscle contracts, the hair stands up and the skin around it bumps out.

In animals with thick fur, raised hair enlarges the layer of air that insulates the body. Without a coat, human goosebumps were long seen as a useless leftover of evolution. But a 2020 study in mice found that the same nerve and muscle also switch on the stem cells that grow hair.
Goosebumps are tiny muscles pulling hairs upright; in mice, those muscles and nerves also make hair grow.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Using an electron microscope, Harvard researchers saw that the sympathetic nerve’s fibres don’t just reach the muscle: they wrap around the stem cells of the hair follicle, the structure a hair grows from, like a ribbon. Under prolonged cold, the nerve became far more active, the stem cells woke up and new hair grew. When the scientists removed the muscle, the nerve pulled back and lost its link to the stem cells. In other words, the goosebump muscle acts as a bridge. The findings, published in the journal Cell, come from mice.

We also get goosebumps hearing an anthem on a podium, walking down the aisle or watching a horror film. In those moments adrenaline steps in, a stress hormone that, among many other effects, makes the skin’s muscles contract.

The idea that human goosebumps do nothing is being questioned. One study recorded 1,198 episodes in eight volunteers and found that they followed drops in skin temperature and came with a slight warming of the skin. It concludes that human goosebumps are not purely vestigial, meaning not just a leftover with no job. But the sample is small, and in humans their role is still uncertain.
Goosebumped skin looks like the skin of a plucked bird. Charles Darwin was already writing about goosebumps in his work on evolution.
